blindSummary:
This is a dangerous destination for transgender visitors and deteriorating fast. In September 2024 parliament passed, modelled on a law in force in a large neighbouring state, a sweeping package banning legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, LGBT public assembly and dissemination of LGBT information — the region's harshest legislative package outside that neighbouring state itself. One day after passage, one of the country's best-known transgender women was stabbed to death in her apartment in the capital; mourners and a major wire service drew a direct line between the law's rhetoric and the killing.

This compounds an existing pattern: the 2021 ransacking of pride organisers' offices by a far-right mob while police stood by, a 'foreign agents' registration law choking LGBT NGOs (which refuse to register and face bankruptcy), and documented failure to protect demonstrators (a group of judgments against the state at a regional human-rights court, still unimplemented). The country's visible trans community is now legally erased and physically targeted.

For a visitor: being visibly trans here now carries both statutory risk (assembly and information provisions) and elevated street-violence risk, with police as unreliable protectors.
blindOutOfScope: The 2024 law's healthcare and gender-recognition provisions are resident-facing; its assembly and information provisions can reach visitors.
blindSourceSummaries: Foreign public broadcaster (Sept 2024): a 37-year-old trans model and influencer, one of the country's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her capital flat one day after parliament passed the sweeping anti-LGBT family-values bill (84-0). Rights groups linked the killing to the government's promotion of the law; the president called it 'horrendous'. The law bans same-sex marriage, gender-affirming surgeries, adoption by non-heterosexual people and 'promotion' of same-sex relationships in schools.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2025 (covering 2024), chapter on this country: the 'foreign agents' registration law endangers LGBTI service provision (organisations refusing to register as 'foreign agents' face fines and bankruptcy); the anti-LGBTI law eroded trust, decreasing service applications; large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing the country and seeking asylum documentation; misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

Local LGBTI organisations' joint report (August 2024) to a regional human-rights body's committee of ministers on implementation of a group of regional-court judgments against this state (failure to protect demonstrators from homophobic/transphobic violence): ineffective investigations into police misconduct; risk of statutes of limitations expiring; new regressive anti-LGBTI legislative initiatives.

News outlet feature (May 2012): this country's laws discriminate against transgender people - legal activists say the law should be changed to allow gender recognition; job applications become difficult when a person's gender identity does not match official paperwork - trans-specific legal barriers.

International human-rights organisations' joint report (May 2003) to a UN child-rights treaty body on the rights of the child in this country: covers discrimination, torture protections, violence and sexual abuse, juvenile justice - general human-rights context including institutionalisation.

Regional media outlet (June 2019): the interior ministry declared holding the capital's pride event 'impossible' in the planned city-centre locations 'due to safety risks'; organisers reported pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel; far-right groups had vowed to thwart the country's first pride event - state obstruction of LGBT assembly.
blindLocalsOnly: The 2024 law's gender-recognition ban and transition-healthcare ban are resident-facing; its assembly and information provisions can reach visitors.
